blocks.text: **The problem.** Like Search in Rotated Sorted Array, but the array may contain **duplicates**. Given the rotated array `nums` and a `target`, return `true` if the target is in it and `false` otherwise. Try to keep the number of steps as small as possible.

blocks.alt: The array 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 searched for 0. The low end, the middle and the high end all hold 1, so there's no way to tell which half is sorted: the 0 could be on either side. The only safe move is to drop both ends, which are 1 and not the target, and look again.

blocks.text: The idea: shrink when the ends tie

The one-pass search from the previous lesson decides which half is sorted by comparing `nums[low]` with `nums[mid]`. With duplicates that can fail: when `nums[low] == nums[mid] == nums[high]`, the seam could be on either side — `[1, 0, 1, 1, 1]` and `[1, 1, 1, 0, 1]` look the same from those three positions. But both ends equal `nums[mid]`, which isn't the target, so they can be **dropped** safely: `low++`, `high--`. In every other case, one side is still provably sorted and the usual logic works.

blocks.code:
def search(nums, target):
    return target in nums

blocks.caption: When low, mid and high hold the same value, drop both ends; otherwise search the sorted half.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n) on average, O(n) in the worst case; space O(1).** An array like `[1, 1, 1, …, 1, 0, 1, 1]` can force a tie at almost every step, and each tie removes only two values. No algorithm can do better in the worst case: if the array is all 1s but one, you might have to look at every value to find the odd one out. That's the follow-up interviewers ask about.

blocks.alt: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space. Binary search + shrink: O(log n) avg, O(n) worst time, O(1) space.
